samples.task_summary: Predict whether a respondent has diabetes from BRFSS survey and health-history features in a way that should generalize across domains.

scores.rationale: Poor physical health days is a robust diabetes correlate and likely generalizes across settings.
Hypertension is a strong, clinically stable comorbidity associated with diabetes risk.
Recent cholesterol screening reflects preventive care and risk burden, but is somewhat care-access dependent.
History of high cholesterol is a durable metabolic risk marker with good cross-domain relevance.
BMI is one of the strongest and most stable predictors of diabetes across populations.
BMI category captures the same core obesity signal in a more coarse but still highly stable way.
Smoking history is relevant but only moderately predictive for diabetes and less direct than metabolic factors.
Current smoking status adds some health-behavior signal, but is weaker and more domain-sensitive than core clinical features.
Stroke history indicates vascular disease and comorbidity burden, but is less directly tied to diabetes than obesity or hypertension.
Coronary heart disease or MI is a stable cardiovascular comorbidity associated with diabetes.
Fruit intake is a weak proxy for diet quality and often noisy across survey domains.
Vegetable intake is similarly a weak, noisy lifestyle proxy with limited marginal stability.
Alcohol quantity is only loosely related to diabetes and is prone to measurement noise and domain shift.
Binge drinking is a behavioral proxy with limited direct predictive value for diabetes.
Physical activity is relevant to diabetes risk, but self-report noise and heterogeneity reduce stability.
Income captures socioeconomic risk and access to care, but is a demographic shortcut and less semantically direct.
Marital status is a weak demographic proxy with limited stable causal relevance.
Routine checkup timing reflects healthcare engagement and access, giving moderate but indirect predictive signal.
Education is a socioeconomic proxy that may correlate with diabetes but is a brittle shortcut.
Health coverage reflects access and age-related structure, useful but partly domain- and policy-dependent.
Mental health burden is associated with chronic disease and can be a reasonably stable health-status marker.
Survey year is a domain identifier and should be strongly downweighted for OOD generalization.
State is highly domain-specific and likely captures geography-specific prevalence and sampling artifacts.
Cost-related unmet care is informative about access and disease management, but is indirect and policy-sensitive.
Sex has some epidemiologic association but is a sensitive demographic attribute and only modestly predictive.

scores.rationale: General self-reported poor physical health is a strong, stable correlate of diabetes burden and complications.
High blood pressure is a robust comorbidity and broadly predictive across populations.
Cholesterol screening history reflects preventive care and risk management, indirectly informative but less direct.
Prior high cholesterol is a strong metabolic risk marker with durable predictive value.
BMI is a core, stable risk factor for diabetes and usually generalizes well.
BMI category captures the same risk signal as BMI with slightly less granularity but good stability.
Smoking history is relevant to health risk but only moderately predictive for diabetes specifically.
Current smoking status adds some behavioral signal, but it is noisier and less directly tied to diabetes.
Stroke history reflects vascular disease burden, which can co-occur with diabetes, but is more downstream.
Coronary heart disease or MI is a meaningful comorbidity and relatively stable health indicator.
Fruit intake is a weak lifestyle proxy with limited direct signal and likely survey noise.
Vegetable intake is similarly a weak, indirect lifestyle marker with modest stable usefulness.
Alcohol quantity may correlate with health behavior, but the relationship to diabetes is inconsistent.
Binge drinking is a brittle behavioral proxy with limited stable predictive value for diabetes.
Physical activity is a plausible protective factor, but self-report noise and heterogeneity reduce reliability.
Income captures socioeconomic status and access, which can matter, but it is a demographic shortcut and domain-sensitive.
Marital status is only weakly related to diabetes and is likely to act as a demographic shortcut.
Routine checkup timing reflects healthcare engagement and access, offering moderate stable signal.
Education is a broad socioeconomic proxy with limited direct biological relevance and shortcut risk.
Health coverage can proxy access and age-related eligibility, but is domain- and policy-sensitive.
Poor mental health days are a stable general health burden marker that can accompany chronic disease.
Survey year is a domain identifier and likely captures temporal artifacts rather than causal risk.
State is a strong domain/location identifier and a brittle shortcut with poor out-of-domain stability.
Cost-related care avoidance reflects access barriers and unmet need, but is somewhat policy- and domain-dependent.
Sex has some epidemiologic association but is a sensitive demographic attribute and weak standalone predictor.

scores.rationale: General self-reported poor physical health is plausibly linked to diabetes and usually stable across domains.
Hypertension is a strong, clinically meaningful comorbidity and tends to generalize well.
Recent cholesterol screening history reflects healthcare engagement and cardiometabolic risk, though somewhat indirect.
High cholesterol history is a strong metabolic risk marker that should remain predictive across settings.
BMI is a core, stable risk factor for diabetes and one of the most useful general predictors.

Smoking history is relevant to health risk but only moderately informative for diabetes specifically.
Current smoking status adds some signal but is weaker and more behaviorally noisy than core metabolic factors.
Stroke history is related to vascular disease and diabetes, but it is less direct and less common.

samples.task_summary: Predict whether a respondent has diabetes using survey, health, and demographic features from BRFSS.

scores.rationale: General poor physical health is a stable proxy for chronic disease burden and diabetes-related morbidity.
Hypertension is a strong, semantically durable comorbidity associated with diabetes risk.
Screening history reflects access and risk management, but is less direct and can shift with healthcare behavior.
High cholesterol history is a robust metabolic comorbidity closely tied to diabetes.
BMI is one of the strongest stable predictors of diabetes risk across domains.
BMI category is highly predictive and usually more stable than raw continuous encoding, though partly redundant with BMI.
Smoking history is relevant to health risk but only weakly and indirectly predictive of diabetes.
Current smoking status adds limited stable signal beyond smoking history and is behaviorally noisy.
Stroke history reflects vascular disease burden and is moderately informative for diabetes.
Coronary heart disease or MI is a strong downstream cardiovascular comorbidity linked to diabetes.
Fruit intake is a weak lifestyle proxy with substantial measurement noise and limited direct predictive power.
Vegetable intake is similarly weak and likely too coarse to contribute much stable signal.
Alcohol quantity is noisy and only weakly related to diabetes in a stable way.
Binge drinking is a broad behavioral marker with limited direct and stable association to diabetes.
Physical activity is a meaningful metabolic risk factor, but self-report noise and coarse coding reduce stability.
Income can proxy access and lifestyle, but it is a demographic shortcut and less semantically direct than health measures.
Marital status may weakly correlate with health behavior and age, but is mostly a brittle demographic proxy.
Recent checkup frequency captures healthcare engagement and access, offering modest stable signal.
Education is a socioeconomic proxy with indirect association to diabetes and potential domain sensitivity.
Insurance coverage reflects access and age structure more than diabetes biology, so it is only modestly useful.
Poor mental health days can correlate with chronic illness burden and self-management challenges, giving moderate stable signal.
Survey year is a domain indicator and risks capturing temporal shifts rather than stable disease predictors.
State is a strong domain identifier and likely encodes sampling, policy, and regional artifacts rather than generalizable biology.
Cost-related unmet care reflects access barriers that can matter, but it is indirect and potentially domain-sensitive.
Sex has some epidemiologic relevance but is a sensitive demographic feature and usually only modestly predictive here.
